newsitem.title: UK: Welsh drinkers poised for Sunday opening victory.
newsitem.headline: Welsh drinkers poised for Sunday opening victory.

text.p: Welsh campaigners said on Tuesday they were poised for final victory in a 35-year battle to get public houses across the country open on Sundays.
They said a referendum which British interior minister Michael Howard ordered to be held on November 6 should mark their final triumph over devout Christians who want to keep the Sabbath drink-free.
Voting will take place in the north-western county of Gwynedd, a bastion of the Welsh language and of the nonconfirmist Christian tradition which was once strongly anti-alcohol.
Until 1961 pubs in most of rural Wales closed on Sundays. Most then changed and since 1989 the town of Dwyfor in Gwynedd has been the last "dry" area of the principality.
"The vote this time will cover the whole of Gwynedd, not just Dwyfor. We are confident of getting a wet Wales at last," said Beuno Hughes of the Seven Day Opening Council pressure group.
Under a law dating from 1961, a referendum on Sunday opening can be held every seven years in any Welsh region if it is requested by at least 500 voters.
"Within Gwynedd as a whole, there was a clear majority for Sunday opening even in 1989," said Hughes.

"And since then the nonconformist tradition has been weakening and people's lifestyles have changed. Sunday is increasingly a day to be with the family and go out for a meal -- washed down by a beer or a glass of wine."
